claims.statement: Selank acetate (TP-7) is not on FDA's active Category 2 list of bulk drug substances presenting significant safety risks; it appears in FDA's separate table of substances that were nominated for the 503A bulks list but subsequently withdrawn by the nominator, where FDA's own safety-risk language (immunogenicity risk from aggregation/peptide-related impurities, and lack of human safety data) still applies.

FDA lacks important information regarding any safety issues raised by selank acetate administered to humans.

claims.statement: According to Kolomin et al.'s review of synthetic peptide anxiolytics, selank is a synthetic heptapeptide (H-Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro-OH) developed by Russian researchers as a protease-resistant analog of the endogenous tetrapeptide tuftsin, engineered by extending tuftsin with a C-terminal Pro-Gly-Pro sequence for stability; it was registered by the Russian Federation Ministry of Health in 2009 and marketed there as a 0.15% intranasal drop formulation.

extractedEvidence.quote: The result was а heptapeptide containing the sequence Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg elongated with the C-terminal part of the tripeptide Pro-Gly-Pro, which proved to be most suitable for the stabilization of the molecule and enhanced its resistance to proteases. The resulting peptide, H-Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro-OH, which was named Selank, had a pronounced anxiolytic activity.
In 2009, the drug was registered by the Russian Federation Ministry of Health and approved for medical use.

reviewFlags: review-article source hosted on a PDF aggregator (semanticscholar.org cache) rather than the publisher site; verify against the original journal record
Russian Ministry of Health registration is not an FDA approval and confers no U.S. regulatory status

Independent review note: an independent primary-literature abstract (PMID 18661785) and Wikipedia's Selank article both corroborate the tuftsin-derivation and heptapeptide sequence description. However, the specific '2009 Russian Ministry of Health registration' date and the '0.15% intranasal drop' formulation detail could not be confirmed from any source independent of this packet's own review-article citation (kolomin-review-synthetic-peptides) in this review pass; those two sub-facts remain single-sourced and should stay flagged pending an independent registry or label source.

claims.statement: A proposed mechanism for Selank's anxiolytic activity is inhibition of enkephalin-degrading enzymes (carboxy- and dipeptidylcarboxypeptidases) in blood plasma, prolonging enkephalin circulation and thereby increasing functional activity of the endogenous opioid system; in vitro plasma assays reported dose-dependent inhibition of Leu-enkephalin breakdown with an IC50 of approximately 15 uM.

extractedEvidence.quote: Selank increases the functional activity of the endogenous opioid system, thereby prolonging the circulation time of enkephalins in the blood.
Selank can be considered a relatively selective inhibitor of carboxy- and dipeptidylcarboxypeptidases of blood plasma, which cleave Leu-enkephalin.

Heptapeptide Selank (Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro), which attenuates behavioral anxiety reactions and does not cause side effects typical of most anxiolytics, dose-dependently inhibited enzymatic hydrolysis of plasma enkephalin (IC50 15 microM). Selank was more potent than peptidase inhibitors bacitracin and puromycin in inhibiting enkephalinases.

claims.statement: Selank has been studied in Russian-language clinical literature as an anxiolytic for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and neurasthenia. The principal trial record (PMID 18454096) is inaccessible via PubMed's public abstract page (bot-check), but its abstract was independently retrieved via the Europe PMC REST API: 62 patients with GAD and neurasthenia were studied, with selank (30 patients) compared against the benzodiazepine medazepam (32 patients) using psychometric scales (Hamilton, Zung, CGI) and plasma enkephalin activity measurements; the abstract reports similar anxiolytic effects between the two arms, with selank additionally showing antiasthenic and psychostimulant effects. A related human study examining patients with anxiety and phobic disorders (per DSM-IV criteria) links plasma enkephalin-degrading enzyme inhibition to symptom improvement. Randomization method, blinding status, and quantitative effect-size statistics are not stated in the retrieved abstract and remain unconfirmed.

claims.statement: Commercial peptide-vendor content markets Selank as producing anxiolytic effects 'comparable to benzodiazepines' with 'no dependence' or withdrawal risk, framing it as a direct benzodiazepine substitute. Independently retrieved trial data (PMID 18454096, via Europe PMC) show one small (N=62), single-country active-comparator study of selank vs. the benzodiazepine medazepam with unknown randomization/blinding status and no independent replication — not the 'no controlled comparison exists' picture, but also nowhere near the support needed for a blanket 'matches benzodiazepines' substitution claim. Critically, dependence and withdrawal risk were not assessed in that trial at all, so the vendor's specific 'no dependence' claim has zero supporting data of any kind from the human literature reviewed here.

conflicts.summary: Independently re-fetched the live FDA bulk drug substances page on 2026-08-29: Selank acetate (TP-7) remains in the 'nominated but withdrawn' table, not the active Category 2 list, with the same immunogenicity/lack-of-human-safety-data language quoted in the packet. The 2026 trade-press reporting (e.g., Lexology, RAPS) on FDA removing/reviewing peptides from the active Category 2 list concerns that separate list only and does not affect Selank's withdrawn-nominations listing; the earlier framing conflating the two lists has been tightened accordingly.

The principal Russian-language GAD/neurasthenia trial (PMID 18454096) was previously believed retrievable only as a translated title/citation; an independent Europe PMC REST API fetch (2026-08-29) retrieved its abstract, showing N=62 (30 selank vs. 32 medazepam, an active benzodiazepine comparator) with similar anxiolytic effects reported. Randomization, blinding, and effect-size statistics remain unstated in that abstract, and dependence/withdrawal risk was never assessed in the trial at all, so vendor marketing's blanket 'matches benzodiazepines, no dependence' framing still overstates what this one small, unreplicated trial supports. This gap between marketed confidence and the now-available (but still thin) trial detail remains a field-authority-gated item pending the full original article.
